newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Digital first quarter results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Digital first quarter results.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp. said Thursday it earned $51 million in its third quarter, down sharply from $124 million a year earlier but slightly better than what Wall Street had expected.
The Maynard, Mass.-based manufacturer of computer chips and computer systems and provider of computer services said its sales fell to $3.3 billion from $3.6 billion.

Digital said the profits were equal to 27 cents a share, down from 74 cents a share a year earlier. Analysts had forecast that Digital would earn 24 cents a share, according to estimates compiled by First Call.

"Even though these results were in-line with our expectations for the quarter, I am not satisfied with our revenue performance," Digital Chief Executive Robert Palmer told reporters on a telephone conference call.
Revenue from sales of products fell to $1.84 billion from $2.06 billion and revenue from services fell to $1.48 billion from $1.57 billion.

Unit sales of computer systems powered by Digital's Alpha microprocessor rose 6 percent in the third quarter over the second quarter, but revenues dropped 2 percent due to competitive price cuts announced in January, Digital said.
Analysts applauded the better-than-expected results, and Digital's stock surged $2.25 to $28.25 a share in mid-afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The fact that Digital could make a measurable profit during the third quarter...I think that's a good sign," said Terry Shannon, editor of a twice-monthly newsletter about Digital."
"They've done a real good job cutting costs, what they have to do now is expand their market" and increase revenues, he added.

Palmer acknowledged during the conference call that industry-leader Sun Microsystems Inc. and other competitors were catching up with Digital's edge in performance with its Alpha microprocessor, and therefore the company must raise its marketing efforts.

Earlier this month, the computer giant announced another restructuring, naming the head of its personal computer unit, Bruce Claflin, as chief of sales and marketing. Palmer said the reorganization should help boost sales and improve its widely-criticized marketing efforts.

"We need to be more effective in our marketing and selling and the new organization should affect that," Palmer said. "I believe that we will continue to improve our earnings and begin to grow our business in the coming quarters," he added.
Analysts believe Digital has good products and services, but the company has been plagued by poor marketing, and sales have been hurt by successive reorganizations.

Fluctuations in the value of the dollar and other currencies cost Digital, which derives roughly two-thirds of its revenues overseas, more than $60 million in the third quarter, Chief Financial Officer Vincent Mullarkey said.
The strong dollar will impact fourth quarter earnings by the same amount or more, he added.
Palmer said Digital is making progress in a number of areas, including its Internet business, where total revenues have grown to more than $1 billion annually.

The company also said it is making progress in sales to Internet service providers, as over 200 in 37 countries are using Digital's server computers running Alpha and Intel processors, its storage systems and networking products.
Mullarkey said the restructuring should warrant improved performance in the upcoming fourth quarter.

"Expectations are that we will have a sequential revenue increase ... a good solid continuation of gross margin improvement, profit improvement, and of course, continued balance sheet improvement," he said.
